intro: Madrid's most remarkable trees are almost all immigrants, brought in by royal gardeners testing whether foreign species could survive freezing winters and scorching, dry summers. A Mexican swamp cypress has outlasted every native tree in the city's most famous park. A Himalayan cedar, an Atlas Mountains cedar, and a Caucasus elm all found the Madrid plateau survivable enough to grow for centuries. Even the city's oldest documented holm oak, one of the few genuinely native species here, grows wild in what was once a royal hunting ground. Spain's Regional Catalogue of Singular Trees protects every one of them.
meta_description: Madrid's remarkable trees are mostly foreign transplants: a Mexican cypress, a Himalayan cedar, a Caucasus elm. Seventeen, catalogued and protected.
question_answer: Madrid's oldest tree, by most accounts, is the Ahuehuete, a Montezuma cypress in the Parterre garden of Retiro Park, though its exact age is genuinely disputed: legend and old guidebooks claim it was planted in 1633, which would make it almost 400 years old, while recent studies by city arborists suggest it may be a much younger 200 years or less. Either way it stands in the Parterre, a five minute walk from Puerta de Alcala.
question_meta: Madrid's oldest tree is a disputed-age Mexican cypress in Retiro Park, claimed at 400 years but possibly 200. Its story and sixteen more trees.
question_context: The Ahuehuete of the Parterre carries two irreconcilable stories about its own age. Guidebooks and the sign at its base repeat a long-standing claim that it was planted in 1633, during the creation of the Retiro as a royal hunting estate under the Count-Duke of Olivares, which would make it close to 400 years old and the oldest tree in Madrid by a wide margin. Specialists, including technicians from Madrid's own city council, are skeptical: the Parterre garden itself was laid out in 1714, replacing whatever vegetation existed before, and some estimates place the tree's planting after 1814, closer to two centuries old rather than four. Montezuma cypresses are native to Mexican wetlands and can live for millennia in the right conditions, so age alone cannot settle the question from the tree's condition. What is not disputed is the species: a swamp cypress from a country most Madrid residents have never associated with their own most famous park, thriving on the plateau for at least two centuries. Getting there: Puerta de Alcala, then a five minute walk into the Parterre garden.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Madrid?
faq.a: Probably the Ahuehuete, a Montezuma cypress in Retiro Park's Parterre garden, though its age is disputed between a legendary 1633 planting date and a more conservative recent estimate of around 200 years.

faq.q: Where is the best place to see old trees in Madrid?
faq.a: Retiro Park, which holds nine of the seventeen trees on this list, more than any other single site, including the Ahuehuete, a Himalayan cedar, a three-trunked yew and a grove of bald cypresses.

faq.q: Are Madrid's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Most are. Retiro Park, Casa de Campo, Campo del Moro and Parque del Oeste are all free public parks. The Royal Botanic Garden charges general admission.

faq.q: Why are so many of Madrid's remarkable trees foreign species?
faq.a: Spanish royal gardeners spent three centuries importing trees from across the world to test what could survive Madrid's climate. Several of the survivors, a Mexican cypress, a Himalayan cedar, a Caucasus elm, are now among the city's oldest and most protected specimens.

trees.name: The Ahuehuete of the Parterre

location.address: Jardin del Parterre, Parque del Retiro, 28009 Madrid

trees.story: This tree carries two stories about its own birth that cannot both be true. The popular version, repeated in guidebooks and on the sign at its base, says it was planted in 1633 when the Count-Duke of Olivares opened the grounds that became Retiro Park, which would make it nearly 400 years old and Madrid's unrivalled oldest tree. Madrid's own municipal arborists are skeptical: the Parterre garden around it was completely replanted in 1714, and some specialists place the tree's actual origin after 1814, closer to two centuries old rather than four. Called Ahuehuete, from the Nahuatl for old man of the water, or simply El Abuelo, the grandfather, it is a Montezuma cypress, a species native to Mexican wetlands where individual specimens are known to live for millennia and reach trunk diameters wider than a house. In arid, landlocked Madrid it has thrived regardless of which age is correct, its buttressed trunk and feathery foliage looking more at home beside a Mexican river than beside a formal Spanish parterre.
trees.transport: Retiro (Metro L2) or Puerta de Alcala, 5 min walk

photo.attribution: UAM Biblioteca y Archivo, Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: Age is presented as a range because sources genuinely and substantially disagree (1633 legend vs. post-1814 estimates from city technicians), per the site's honesty standard rather than picking one figure. Coordinates corrected 2026-07-26 to the tree's own OpenStreetMap node (id 4565394685, "Ahuehuete del Parterre"), which independently corroborates a Comunidad de Madrid singular-tree ficha reporting near-identical coordinates (40.41564, -3.68798) for the same tree. Photo URL fixed 2026-07-28: the stored thumb path (commons/thumb/e/e4/...) 404'd, a genuine dead link caught by a site-wide approved-photo spot-check, not just a rate limit; Commons' own API gives this exact filename's real path as f/f2, fetched and viewed directly there to confirm it is still the same fenced, multi-trunked Ahuehuete before swapping the URL.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Crystal Palace

location.address: Paseo Julio Romero de Torres, Parque del Retiro, 28009 Madrid

trees.story: This cedar stands directly in front of the pond at the Palacio de Cristal, a 19th century glass and iron pavilion built in 1887 to exhibit plants and animals brought back from the Philippines, and it has spent most of the pavilion's history as part of the same postcard view: the glass palace reflected in the water, framed by the cedar's dark, tiered branches. Deodar cedars come from the western Himalayas, where the name deodar derives from a Sanskrit phrase meaning timber of the gods, and the species reached European ornamental gardens in the early 19th century as one of many exotic conifers collectors raced to introduce. Madrid's climate, hot and dry in summer rather than the Himalayan cedar's native monsoon-fed mountains, has suited this specimen well enough that it now ranks among Retiro's six officially singular trees, protected under the same regional catalogue as its more famous neighbour, the disputed-age Ahuehuete a short walk away.
trees.transport: Ibiza (Metro L9) or Retiro (Metro L2), 8 min walk
trees.notes: Age is an estimate based on the Palacio de Cristal's 1887 construction date and typical planting-alongside-building practice; no source gives a precise planting date for this specific tree. Pin moved 2026-07-27 about 160m to the Palacio de Cristal building itself, still an anchor rather than a surveyed point. Resolved to confirmed 2026-07-29: an individually-tagged OpenStreetMap node named "Cedro del Himalaya" (Spanish for this exact species) sits on Paseo Julio Romero de Torres, the pond-side walkway immediately beside the Palacio de Cristal, about 30m from mad_004's already-confirmed Bald Cypress pin in the same pond and roughly 115m from the prior building-level anchor. A second "Cedro del Himalaya" node exists elsewhere in Retiro (Paseo de Lagasca, over 700m away, clearly a different specimen) and was not used.

trees.name: The Three-Trunked Yew of the Velazquez Palace

location.address: Palacio de Velazquez, Parque del Retiro, 28009 Madrid

trees.story: Rather than one trunk, this yew splits into three, each thick enough to measure separately: 142, 120 and 140 centimetres around, fused into a single crown 18 metres wide standing beside the eastern wall of the Palacio de Velazquez, a red-brick exhibition hall built in 1883. European yews are famously slow growing and long lived, capable of reaching ages in the thousands of years in the right conditions, and famously toxic in almost every part except the flesh around the seed, a combination that has made the species a fixture of European churchyards for centuries, planted as much for its poison as its evergreen symbolism. At only 12 metres tall despite its age, this specimen shows the yew's characteristic patience: slow vertical growth traded for density and longevity. A wooden fence now rings the tree for its protection, a modest concession for one of only six trees in the whole of Retiro Park to hold official singular tree status from the Community of Madrid.
trees.notes: Coordinates corrected 2026-07-26 to the tree's own OpenStreetMap node (id 3497610360, named "Tejo del Palacio de Velázquez del Retiro", an exact name match to this tree and its Spanish Wikipedia article). Photo (iNaturalist observation 307498789, 13-15m from the confirmed pin, tagged cultivated) viewed directly: dense yew foliage with multiple visible trunks, consistent with the tree's own three-trunked description.

trees.name: The Bald Cypresses of the Crystal Palace Pond

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn copper and drop, doubled in the pond the trees grow from

location.address: Estanque del Palacio de Cristal, Parque del Retiro, 28009 Madrid

trees.story: Several bald cypresses grow directly out of the pond in front of the Palacio de Cristal, their trunks and lower roots permanently submerged, a planting scheme that only works because this particular conifer, unlike almost every other cone-bearing tree, tolerates and even prefers standing water. Bald cypresses develop distinctive above-water root growths called pneumatophores, sometimes called cypress knees, that let the roots breathe oxygen the flooded soil cannot supply, an adaptation evolved in the swamps of the southeastern United States rather than anywhere near Madrid. Planted around 1918, roughly three decades after the glass pavilion itself went up in 1887, the grove has grown into one of the more unusual sights in a park otherwise dominated by conventional planting: full-grown conifers standing calf-deep in a reflecting pool, doubling their own image in the water they grow from. One specimen among the group carries the Community of Madrid's singular tree designation, protecting a planting choice that was, by the standards of 1918 Spanish gardening, a genuine experiment.
trees.transport: Ibiza (Metro L9) or Retiro (Metro L2), 8 min walk
trees.notes: This entry represents the grove of bald cypresses in the pond as a group, of which one specific specimen holds official singular tree status; sources do not distinguish which exact tree in the group carries the designation. Coordinates corrected 2026-07-26 to OpenStreetMap's own node for this tree (id 3919471940, named "Ciprés Calvo del Estanque del Palacio de Cristal", matching this entry's Spanish Wikipedia source), which at least pins the specific specimen the community has mapped under that name, even though which physical trunk in the pond that corresponds to is still not independently surveyed.

trees.name: The Cypress of the Royal Botanic Garden

location.address: Real Jardin Botanico, Plano de la Flor terrace, Plaza de Murillo 2, 28014 Madrid

trees.story: This cypress has stood on the Plano de la Flor terrace since before the Royal Botanic Garden moved to its current site. King Carlos III relocated the garden here in 1781, transplanting an existing scientific collection to sit beside his new Prado promenade, and this cypress, already growing or planted around that time, has outlasted every institutional change since: French occupation during the Peninsular War, a 19th century closure and near-abandonment, and a 20th century restoration that returned the garden to something close to its original Enlightenment-era design. At 32 metres it is both the oldest and the tallest tree in a garden that exists specifically to hold record specimens, and its trunk, a metre and a half across, has grown thick enough that the tree is now folded into the Paisaje de la Luz, Landscape of Light, the cultural corridor linking the Prado, the botanic garden and the Retiro that UNESCO named a World Heritage Site in 2021.
trees.access: Paid entry to the Royal Botanic Garden
trees.transport: Atocha (Metro L1) or Banco de Espana (Metro L2), 8 min walk
trees.notes: Coordinates corrected 2026-07-26 to the tree's own OpenStreetMap node (id 3170278091, "Ciprés del Real Jardín Botánico"), inside the garden on the Plano de la Flor terrace rather than the garden's street entrance.

trees.name: The Caucasian Elm of the Botanic Garden

location.address: Real Jardin Botanico, Paseo de Mutis (north zone), Plaza de Murillo 2, 28014 Madrid

trees.story: Measured against every other tree in the Royal Botanic Garden, this one wins on height, reaching by some counts over 30 metres in the garden's north zone along the Paseo de Mutis, tall enough that garden staff and visiting botanists disagree on the exact figure by several metres depending on measurement method. The species itself, Zelkova carpinifolia, comes from mountain forests spanning Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Turkey and Iran, and only reached European gardens in the 18th century as part of the same wave of scientific plant collecting that filled Madrid's garden with foreign specimens under royal sponsorship. This particular tree is roughly two centuries old, meaning it has spent essentially its entire life as the garden's tallest resident, a distinction the fast-growing species tends to earn early and keep. It carries singular tree designation number 260 in the Community of Madrid's regional catalogue, one number among 280 protected specimens across the wider region.
trees.access: Paid entry to the Royal Botanic Garden
trees.transport: Atocha (Metro L1) or Banco de Espana (Metro L2), 8 min walk
trees.notes: Coordinates corrected 2026-07-26 to the tree's own OpenStreetMap node (id 3170278093, "Olmo del Caúcaso del Real Jardín Botánico", tagged Zelkova carpinifolia matching this entry's species).

trees.name: The Holm Oak of the Trillo Roundabout

location.address: Glorieta del Trillo, Casa de Campo, 28011 Madrid

trees.story: Roads converge on this tree rather than around it. The Glorieta del Trillo, where the Carretera de Somosaguas, the Paseo de los Castanos and the Camino de Rodajos all meet inside Casa de Campo, is named for the holm oak growing at its centre, a roughly 300 year old specimen with a crown 18.5 metres across and a trunk 4.6 metres around. Casa de Campo itself was a royal hunting estate from the 16th century until 1931, when the Second Republic opened it to the public, which means this oak spent roughly two centuries of its life on private land reserved for the Spanish crown's deer and boar hunts rather than growing in anything resembling a public park. Holm oaks are Iberia's signature evergreen, slow growing and built to survive exactly the hot, dry summers and cold winters Madrid delivers, and this one has outlasted the hunting estate, the monarchy that owned it, and the Republic that opened the gates, still marking the same road junction today.
trees.transport: Casa de Campo (Metro L5/L10), 20 min walk or park shuttle
trees.notes: Pin was genuinely wrong, not just approximate: the previous coordinates, converted from a sourced DMS reading (40°24'58.2"N 3°44'46.3"W), sat about 600m from the tree's actual position. Corrected 2026-07-27 via an OpenStreetMap node individually named "Encina del Trillo," tagged as a Comunidad de Madrid natural monument with species Quercus ilex and an 18.5m crown diameter, an exact match to this entry's own '18.5 metres across' figure. Two more nearby OSM features (a "Glorieta del Trillo" locality node and its own information board) corroborate the same cluster.

trees.name: The Aleppo Pine of Campo del Moro

location.address: Jardines del Campo del Moro, north zone, 28005 Madrid

trees.story: This pine grows in the gardens spread beneath the Royal Palace's western facade, a formal landscape that took its current shape only in the 1890s even though the land had belonged to the crown for centuries before that, used variously as a hunting ground, a military exercise field and, briefly, a source of building stone. At 30 metres tall with a trunk 2.55 metres around, the pine ranks among six officially singular trees inside Campo del Moro's twenty hectares, sharing that status with a stone pine, an oak, a coast redwood and a pair of yews scattered through the same grounds. Aleppo pines are a Mediterranean basin native, drought tolerant and comfortable in Madrid's dry summers in a way many of the garden's more exotic imports are not, which may explain why this specimen has reached such size in only a century and a half, a fraction of the multi-century ages claimed for some of the city's other singular trees.
trees.notes: Coordinates are an estimate for the garden's north zone, where sources place the tree; no surveyed point was found.

trees.name: The Grandfather Cedar of Parque del Oeste

location.address: Parque del Oeste, near Avenida de Ruperto Chapi, 28008 Madrid

trees.story: Known locally as El Abuelo, the grandfather, this Atlas cedar grows near the Fuente de la Salud and the artificial stream that cuts through the northern part of Parque del Oeste, a park built on former rubbish dumps and quarry land at the turn of the 20th century and rebuilt again after Civil War fighting damaged it in the 1930s. Atlas cedars are native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria and reached European gardens as an ornamental import around 1840, which sets an outer limit on how old any specimen in Madrid could plausibly be; the species itself is capable of living centuries, some specialists say close to a thousand years under ideal conditions, though this individual tree's precise age has not been established by any source found. What is established is its status: one of the Community of Madrid's officially catalogued singular trees, numbered and registered like the 279 other specimens across the region, marking it as protected regardless of whether its exact birth year is ever pinned down.

photo.attribution: Luis Fernandez Garcia, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: No source found gives a specific planting date or precise current age for this tree; the age range given is bounded only by the species' 1840 introduction to Europe and general knowledge of Atlas cedar growth rates, stated honestly as an estimate rather than a researched figure. Coordinates corrected 2026-07-26 to a named "Cedro del Atlas" node in OpenStreetMap (id 10261810384), the only tree in Parque del Oeste tagged with that Spanish common name, about 300m from the previous estimate but inside the same park and consistent with the Fuente de la Salud/Ruperto Chapi area sources describe. Photo added 2026-07-29: File:Cedrus atlantica 20090311.jpg (CC BY 3.0), whose own Commons description explicitly names Cedrus atlantica, Parque del Oeste, Madrid. Downloaded and personally viewed: a genuine, correctly-identified Atlas cedar branch and needle close-up, species confirmed by the silvery-blue needle clusters. Held at found_needs_check rather than approved: the photo carries no GPS data and is a needle macro with no trunk or landmark in frame, so it cannot positively confirm this is El Abuelo specifically rather than another Atlas cedar elsewhere in the park (OSM shows only one tree named that way, which favours it being the same tree, but the photo itself can't prove it).

trees.name: The Stone Pine of the Priest's House

location.address: El Capricho, Paseo de la Alameda de Osuna, 28042 Madrid

trees.story: This stone pine grows half hidden among shrubs near a small hermitage called the Casa del Cura, the priest's house, in a park built for a duchess rather than a king. Maria Josefa Pimentel, Duchess of Osuna, commissioned El Capricho in 1784, hiring French landscape designers Jean-Baptiste Mulot and Pierre Provost to lay out French, English and Italian style gardens across fourteen hectares in what was then open countryside east of Madrid, now the Barajas district near the airport that shares its name. The pine likely dates from that same late 18th century construction period, making it a contemporary of the duchess's original vision rather than a later addition. Unlike Madrid's grander royal gardens, El Capricho suffered decades of neglect and, during the Spanish Civil War, served as a military command post, before the city restored it and reopened it to visitors in the 1990s. The pine survived all of it, one of the park's few catalogued singular trees and among the oldest living witnesses to the duchess's original 18th century design.
trees.access: Free, but visitor numbers are limited and advance booking is recommended; closed Mondays and Tuesdays
trees.transport: Canillejas (Metro L5), 15 min walk, or El Capricho (Metro L5), 5 min walk
trees.notes: Age is estimated from the park's known 1784-1839 construction period rather than a specific planting-date source. Location corrected 2026-07-28: a geocode audit flagged the stored coordinate as roughly 1.4km from El Capricho. Nominatim's own geocode of the park's official name, "Jardin historico El Capricho de la Alameda Osuna," places it at 40.4563, -3.5980, matching the Barajas neighbourhood already stated here. Moved onto the park; still approximate since no source gives the Casa del Cura hermitage's own position within it. Photo added 2026-07-29: an iNaturalist CC BY observation (Cenaida, 22 Sept 2024, id 243394911) of a Pinus pinea inside El Capricho, viewed directly and confirmed as a genuine stone-pine photo taken in a shrubby, wooded corner of the park. Held at found_needs_check rather than approved because the park's own documentation describes several catalogued stone pines near the Casa del Cura meadow, and this photo's generic place_guess cannot confirm it is specifically the one singled out as the singular specimen rather than one of its neighbours. A 2026-07-31 session with working image tooling rendered it directly and agrees with this read: the frame shows two to three similar stone-pine trunks together from below, with no way to tell which, if any, is the catalogued specimen rather than a neighbour. Left at found_needs_check; this is an identity question a photo can't settle, not a framing or quality one, so a future session would need a source that individually locates the catalogued tree before promoting any photo here.

trees.name: The Strawberry Tree of the Plaza de la Lealtad

location.address: Plaza de la Lealtad, south side facing the Ritz, 28014 Madrid

trees.story: Madrid's coat of arms shows a bear reaching up into a strawberry tree, and this is the closest thing the city has to the original. It stands in the southern corner of the Plaza de la Lealtad, opposite the Ritz, propped on iron crutches installed when its own limbs grew heavy enough to threaten pulling it over. Strawberry trees are usually shrubs, three or four metres of Mediterranean scrub. This one has been allowed to grow into an actual tree for more than a century, which is why the props are needed at all. It is also why the Comunidad de Madrid added it to the singular-tree catalogue in 2015 for cultural rather than botanical significance: the emblem, made real. Historians are fairly sure the heraldic tree of 1222 was never a madrono in the first place and that the bear on the crest was reaching for something else entirely, but the city has committed. The fruit is the payoff. Through November and December it carries white bell flowers and the previous year's fruit at the same time, red warty spheres that look like lychees and taste of very little. The Latin unedo means eat only one.

best_time.label: November and December, when it flowers and ripens last year's fruit at once

trees.transport: Banco de Espana (Metro L2), 3 min walk
trees.notes: Added to the catalogue by ORDEN 68/2015 (Anexo II, Arbutus unedo, Madrid, motivo: significacion cultural). Existence and centenarian age independently confirmed by Telemadrid's August 2024 survey of the 15 singular trees of Retiro, Recoletos and the Prado, which places it in the Plaza de la Lealtad. Pin is approximate: no individually named OpenStreetMap node exists for this tree (the two 'Madrono' nodes in the Overpass extract for this area both sit inside the Retiro and are different trees), so the coordinate anchors the south side of the plaza facing the Ritz, which is where every source places it. The plaza is small and the tree is the only one on crutches, so an approximate pin still finds it.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at the Prado

location.address: Jardines del Museo del Prado, beside the Velazquez statue, Paseo del Prado, 28014 Madrid

trees.story: Nobody agrees how old this cedar is, and the gap is a century. The regional catalogue and the city's tree literature give roughly 120 years. The guides to the Paseo del Prado put it at 232, which would date the planting to within a generation of Juan de Villanueva's museum building. A third account, more plausible than either, ties it to 1871, when the garden on the museum's western slope was laid out around the Velazquez statue. What is not in dispute is the shape: 26 metres tall, a crown 22 metres across and a trunk four and a half metres around, so the tree is nearly as wide as it is high, its upper branches held out in the flat horizontal plates that only old Lebanon cedars make. It stands a few steps from the museum's busiest door, and most of the several million people who pass it every year are looking at the queue. Cedrus libani is the tree of the Phoenician fleets and of Solomon's temple, reduced in its Lebanese homeland to a handful of protected groves. Madrid keeps one on the Paseo del Prado, inside the stretch of city that UNESCO inscribed in 2021.
trees.access: Free, public garden on the Paseo del Prado
trees.transport: Banco de Espana (Metro L2) or Estacion del Arte (Metro L1), 5 min walk
trees.notes: Age is given as a range because the sources genuinely disagree: the singular-tree documentation says about 120 years, Telemadrid's August 2024 survey says 232, and a separate account dates the surrounding garden and its cedars to 1871. Flagged rather than resolved, per the site's honesty standard. Pin comes from the individually named OpenStreetMap node 'Cedro del Libano' carrying Wikidata Q108653756 (40.413975, -3.6927964), which agrees with the published coordinate to about three metres. More than one cedar stands in this garden; the catalogued specimen is the large one beside the Velazquez statue, which is the tree both records point at.

trees.name: The Hackberry of the Plaza de Murillo

location.address: Plaza de Murillo, at the corner of the Museo del Prado, 28014 Madrid

trees.story: The Plaza de Murillo, the small formal square between the Prado's south door and the gate of the Royal Botanic Garden, holds four catalogued conifers and one broadleaf that outgrew every one of them. This hackberry stands 25 metres tall, close to the recorded ceiling for the species, and is about 140 years old, which puts its planting in the decade the square took its present shape. Celtis australis is the almez, a southern European tree with a smooth grey trunk that looks poured rather than grown, and fruit the size of a pea that turns from orange to near black. Spanish villages once coppiced it for the handles of hayforks, because the young wood bends a long way before it snaps, and whole valleys in Aragon lived off that trade. It is also, unglamorously, one of the toughest street trees in existence, indifferent to drought, wind and exhaust, which is exactly why a specimen this size is still standing on an island of pavement in central Madrid. Look for its flowers in April and you will not find them; they are green and smaller than a grain of rice. Stand under it in July, when the stone outside the Prado is at forty degrees, and the reason the square was planted this way needs no explaining.
trees.transport: Estacion del Arte (Metro L1), 4 min walk
trees.notes: Catalogued by the Comunidad de Madrid as 'Almez del Paseo del Prado'; both the Ayuntamiento's Paseo del Prado material and Telemadrid's August 2024 survey place it at the Plaza de Murillo corner of the museum, give the species as Celtis australis and the age as about 140 years with a height of 25 metres. Pin is the individually named OpenStreetMap node 'Almez' tagged denotation=natural_monument at 40.4128287, -3.6924632, which matches the published coordinate exactly. It is the only hackberry at this corner.

trees.name: The Himalayan Spruce of the Plaza de Murillo

location.address: Plaza de Murillo, between the Prado's south facade and the Royal Botanic Garden, 28014 Madrid

trees.story: Of the four conifers catalogued in the Plaza de Murillo, this is the one nobody can name. Picea smithiana grows wild between two and nearly four thousand metres up, in Afghanistan, Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and reached Europe in 1818 when seed arrived in Scotland. It has the longest needles of any spruce and the most extreme weeping habit in the genus: the side branches hang almost vertically off the limbs, so a mature tree looks like it is slowly melting. This one is 22 metres tall with a trunk 1.85 metres around. Its age is honestly unsettled. The city's guides say 140 years; the botanical account attached to the square claims a planting around 1790, which would make it older than the Botanic Garden's present layout and older than nearly anything else rooted along the Paseo del Prado. The species honours Sir James Edward Smith, who founded the Linnean Society and bought Linnaeus's entire collection at twenty-four. Its other name, morinda, is a Himalayan word for flower honey and refers to the resin that beads on the young cones. A high-altitude spruce is the wrong tree for a Madrid summer by every measure that matters, which is what makes it worth standing under.
trees.transport: Estacion del Arte (Metro L1), 4 min walk
trees.notes: Protected by the Comunidad de Madrid since the 1992 decree and carried through into the 2015 consolidated catalogue. Second source is Telemadrid's August 2024 survey (species, location, 22 metres, 140 years); the long-running ArbolesdeMadrid blog independently identifies the specimen and its 1992 protection. Age flagged as a range because the two figures in circulation, about 140 years and a planting around 1790, cannot both be right and neither is sourced to a core count. Pin is the OpenStreetMap node 'Picea del Himalaya' carrying Wikidata Q108653996 (40.4126313, -3.6918174), about six metres from the published coordinate. It is the only Picea smithiana in the square.

trees.name: The Four-Trunked Silver Maple of Cecilio Rodriguez

location.address: Jardines de Cecilio Rodriguez, Parque del Retiro, 28009 Madrid

trees.story: This maple gave up on having one trunk early. It divides at about head height into four main stems, each carrying its share of a crown 15 metres across and 20 metres tall, a form silver maples fall into readily and gardeners usually correct. Nobody corrected this one. It stands inside the Jardines de Cecilio Rodriguez, the walled Andalusian-style garden in the south-east corner of the Retiro, laid out in the 1940s on ground first set aside in 1929 for an extension to the park's zoo. The peacocks that patrol the hedges are what came of that plan instead. Acer saccharinum is North American, a tree of the river bottoms of the eastern United States, and it takes its name from the underside of the leaf rather than from sap: turn one over and it is pale silver white, so a breeze through the crown changes the colour of the entire tree at once. It flowers before it leafs, in tight red clusters in late February, weeks before anything else in the park has woken up. The garden shuts at dusk and is one of the quietest corners of the Retiro, which for a park this busy is worth knowing about.
trees.access: Free, public park. The Cecilio Rodriguez gardens keep shorter hours than the rest of the Retiro and close at dusk
trees.notes: Species is Acer saccharinum, the silver maple, per the Comunidad de Madrid catalogue and the tree's own name; the OpenStreetMap node tags it 'Acer saccharum', which is a different species and is treated here as a tagging error, not a source. Existence and centenarian age confirmed independently by Telemadrid's August 2024 survey, which places it in the Cecilio Rodriguez gardens. Pin is the individually named OpenStreetMap node carrying Wikidata Q108472384 (40.4139598, -3.678499).

trees.name: The Tall Cedar of the Avenida del Peru

location.address: Avenida del Peru at the Plaza de Guatemala, Parque del Retiro, 28009 Madrid

trees.story: At 33 metres this is the tallest tree on the Retiro's catalogued list, and it does not look it, because it stands at a junction of wide avenues where nothing nearby gives the eye anything to measure against. Walk up to the trunk, 3.3 metres around, and the height arrives all at once. It is a Cedar of Lebanon of about 120 years, at the meeting of the Avenida del Peru and the Plaza de Guatemala in the park's north-east, a few paces from the equestrian monument to General Martinez Campos. That statue was unveiled in 1907, when the cedar was already a young tree of perhaps twenty, watching masons set the plinth. Lebanon cedars grow through three clearly different shapes. Young ones are narrow cones, middle-aged ones broaden, and only the old ones flatten into the tiered, table-topped silhouette that ended up on the Lebanese flag. This one is midway through the second stage, still conical at the top and already spreading below. Its crown spans 11 metres against the 22 of the older cedar down at the Prado. The two of them, twenty minutes apart on foot, are the same species caught at two points in a life that can run past a thousand years.
trees.transport: Retiro (Metro L2), 10 min walk into the park, or O'Donnell (Metro L6), 8 min
trees.notes: Catalogued as 'Cedro del Parque del Retiro'. Existence and location independently confirmed by Telemadrid's August 2024 survey, which places a centenarian cedar beside the Martinez Campos monument. Pin is the individually named OpenStreetMap node carrying Wikidata Q108653804 (40.4173579, -3.6808949), about eight metres from the published coordinate. The claim that it is the tallest of the Retiro's catalogued trees is checked against the other Retiro entries in this file and their recorded heights, not asserted city-wide.

trees.name: The Blue Gum North of the Estanque

location.address: North of the Estanque Grande, near the Paseo de Coches, Parque del Retiro, 28009 Madrid

trees.story: In February 2015 the Comunidad de Madrid revised its register of singular trees and published two lists side by side. One added 69 trees. The other struck 43 off, for the blunt reason that they were dead or gone, and among them was the Eucalipto del Parque del Retiro. On the same page, a different eucalyptus a few hundred metres away was written into the catalogue in its place, listed for historical significance. This is the replacement. It stands north of the Estanque Grande, near the Paseo de Coches, over 20 metres tall with a crown about as wide and a trunk you cannot get your arms halfway round. Eucalyptus globulus is Tasmanian, brought to Spain in the 1860s on the theory that it drained marshes and drove off malaria, and planted so enthusiastically across the north-west that it has become a management problem there. In a Madrid park it is simply a giant, its bark peeling away in long ribbons and its leaves smelling of a cough sweet when you crush one. The trunk carries a century of carved initials, which is why the tree writers who have followed it since the 2000s keep asking the park for a sign and a low rail.
trees.notes: This entry is deliberately the replacement, not the tree it replaced. ORDEN 68/2015 Anexo I strikes 'Eucalipto del Parque del Retiro' (Eucalyptus globulus, Madrid) from the catalogue as dead or gone; Anexo II of the same order adds 'Eucalipto azul del Retiro' (Madrid, motivo: significacion historica). Verified alive in August 2024 by Telemadrid's survey of the 15 singular trees of Retiro, Recoletos and the Prado. Pin agrees between the published coordinate and an OpenStreetMap node named 'Eucalipto Azul del Parque del Retiro' with species=globulus and denotation=natural_monument at 40.418848, -3.6821557, about four metres apart. A second OSM node with the same name and Wikidata Q108473045 sits roughly 60 metres south-west; treated as a duplicate record rather than a second tree, since the two published sources both point at the northern position.
